items.followUp: Why are elements of groups 13 and 14 called p-block elements?

rubric.why: Identifies the subshell occupied by the differentiating electron.
rubric.description: States that the differentiating or last electron enters an s orbital.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the s orbital or s subshell.

rubric.why: Connects the group classification to the outer electronic configuration.
rubric.description: Explains that the outermost electron configuration of group 1 and 2 elements involves the s subshell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking groups 1 and 2 to the s subshell.

modelAnswer: In elements of groups 1 and 2, the last electron enters an s orbital.
Therefore, these elements are called s-block elements.

items.followUp: State the octet rule and give one example of an atom attaining an octet.

rubric.why: The rule describes the stable outer-shell electron arrangement.
rubric.description: States that atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the eight-electron arrangement in the outer shell.

rubric.why: Describes how atoms attain the stable arrangement.
rubric.description: States that atoms gain, lose, or share electrons to attain an octet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating an accepted way atoms achieve the octet.

modelAnswer: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to have eight electrons in their outermost shell.
This gives them a stable electronic configuration.

items.followUp: State two conditions needed for the formation of a covalent bond.

rubric.why: Covalent bonding involves electrons from incompletely filled orbitals.
rubric.description: States that the atoms have unpaired electrons in their outer shells or half-filled orbitals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying unpaired electrons or half-filled orbitals.

rubric.why: Overlap and pairing of electrons allow the covalent bond to form.
rubric.description: States that the relevant orbitals overlap and the bonding electrons have opposite spins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating orbital overlap and opposite-spin pairing.

modelAnswer: The combining atoms must have unpaired electrons in their outer shells.
Their half-filled orbitals must overlap, and the electrons forming the bond must have opposite spins.

items.followUp: Write two properties of covalent compounds.

rubric.why: A coordinate bond becomes equivalent to an ordinary covalent bond after formation.
rubric.description: States that a coordinate covalent bond behaves like an ordinary covalent bond once formed.

rubric.why: These are common properties of molecular coordinate-covalent compounds as taught with covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Gives a common physical property, such as low melting and boiling points or poor electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one appropriate property.

modelAnswer: Once formed, a coordinate covalent bond behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.
Coordinate covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points and do not conduct electricity.

items.followUp: What is absolute zero on the Kelvin scale, and what is its value in degrees Celsius?

rubric.why: Defines absolute zero by the limiting thermal motion or energy of particles.
rubric.description: Defines absolute zero as the lowest possible temperature, at which particle motion ceases in the textbook description.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Gives the Celsius value of absolute zero.
rubric.description: States the value as approximately −273 °C (more precisely −273.15 °C).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct Celsius value.

modelAnswer: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, at which molecular motion is considered to cease.

items.followUp: Define crystalline solids and give two examples.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack the long-range regular arrangement of particles found in crystals.
rubric.description: Defines amorphous solids as solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the irregular arrangement.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate recognition of amorphous solids.
rubric.description: Gives examples such as glass, plastic, or rubber.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.
Examples include glass, plastic, and rubber.

items.followUp: How can a saturated solution be prepared by heating and cooling?

rubric.why: Heating allows more solute to dissolve in the solvent.
rubric.description: States that the solvent or solution is heated and solute is added until a hot saturated solution is made.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing preparation of a saturated hot solution.

rubric.why: Cooling without crystallisation can leave more dissolved solute than the solution can normally hold at the lower temperature.
rubric.description: States that the hot saturated solution is cooled carefully, preferably without disturbance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cooling step.

modelAnswer: Heat the solvent and add solute until no more dissolves, making a hot saturated solution.
Cool the solution slowly without disturbance; the resulting solution is supersaturated.

items.followUp: Define volume/volume percent concentration and give an example.

rubric.why: The definition gives the mass of solute relative to the total mass of solution.
rubric.description: Defines m/m percent as the mass of solute in 100 units of mass of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: A numerical example demonstrates use of the mass-percent definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as 10 g solute in 100 g solution giving 10% m/m.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example with the correct percentage.

modelAnswer: m/m % concentration is the mass of solute present in 100 units of mass of solution.
For example, 10 g of solute in 100 g of solution gives a concentration of 10% m/m.
